original_value: Intertidal habitats are among the harshest environments on the planet, and have emerged as a model system for exploring the ecological impacts of global climate change. Deploying reliable instrumentation to measure environmental conditions such as temperature is challenging in this environment. The application of wireless sensor networks (WSNs) shows considerable promise as a means of optimizing continuous data collection, but poor link quality and unstable connections between nodes, caused by harsh physical environmental conditions, bring about a delay problem. In this paper, we model and analyze the components of delays in an intertidal wireless sensor network system (IT-WSN). We show that, by properly selecting routing pathways, it is feasible to improve delay. To this end, we propose a Predictive Delay Optimization (Pido) framework, which provides a new metric for routing path selection. Pido incorporates delay introduced by both link quality and node conditions, and designs a classifier to predict future conditions of nodes, i.e., the likely time of aerial exposure at low tide in this case. We evaluate the performance of Pido in both a real IT-WSN system and a large-scale simulation, the result demonstrates that Pido decreases up to 73% of delays on average with limited overhead.

result.paraphrase: Intertidal habitats are among the planet’s most extreme environments and have become a model system for studying the ecological effects of global climate change. In this setting, deploying dependable instruments to measure environmental conditions such as temperature is difficult. Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) offer strong potential for improving continuous data collection, but poor link quality and unstable node-to-node connections caused by harsh physical conditions create delay problems. In this paper, we model and analyze the delay components of an intertidal wireless sensor network system (IT-WSN). We show that delay can be improved by choosing routing paths appropriately. To that end, we propose a Predictive Delay Optimization (Pido) framework that introduces a new metric for routing-path selection. Pido accounts for delay caused by both link quality and node conditions, and it uses a classifier to predict future node conditions, namely the likely time of aerial exposure at low tide in this case. We evaluate Pido on both a real IT-WSN system and a large-scale simulation, and the results show that Pido reduces delays by up to 73% on average with limited overhead.
